enforced_by.check_secret_exposure.py: Refuses a workflow that could hand signing material to a pull request: a secret in a workflow with a pull_request trigger, pull_request_target at all, or a secret used without an environment to gate it.
enforced_by.what_it_cannot_enforce: Whether a secret is echoed to a log or written into an artifact is a property of what a step does at runtime, not of the workflow file, so no static check can settle it. What is enforced is the part that can be: a secret cannot be reachable from a pull request, and its use must pass an environment gate a reviewer controls. GitHub also masks known secret values in logs, which helps and is not a guarantee -- a transformed secret is not masked. The backup half of the boundary is enforced elsewhere: the purge backup excludes key material, drilled in I4.

key_custody.never: Not in the repository, not in a pull-request job, not echoed to a log, not written into a release artifact, and not included in a purge backup. The first four are enforced by check_secret_exposure.py; the last is already enforced by the purge backup, which excludes key material and is drilled in I4.

primary_in_ci.deadline: v1.0 J10, before the first release anyone relies on
primary_in_ci.does_not_reduce_consequence: The secret is decrypted into the runner at job time and anything executing there can read it: a compromised build dependency, or a mistake in the workflow. Neither involves signing in. If it happens, a primary key means the identity is compromised, not one subkey.
primary_in_ci.reduces_likelihood: Hardware security keys are required to sign in to the account, actions are pinned by digest, the environment admits only main and v* tags, and main is protected against direct pushes. Account takeover -- the likeliest route on a solo project -- is hard.
primary_in_ci.state: accepted for now, revisit before the first published release
primary_in_ci.what: GPG_RELEASE_PRIVATE_KEY holds the primary key, which can certify as well as sign.
primary_in_ci.why_it_is_acceptable_today: The key has signed nothing. No release exists, nobody has fetched this public key, no artifact depends on it -- so reissuing the identity costs one keygen. That cost starts growing when a signed release exists that somebody has verified.

public_key.why_in_the_repository: It travels with the source rather than only with the release. A verifier who fetches the key from the same page as the artifact has verified that the page is self-consistent and very little else; a key that arrived with the source, through a different path and at a different time, is a weaker but genuinely independent anchor.

release_key_is_not_the_evidence_key.why: The evidence reserve signs with a pinned subkey whose primary is offline, and its whole value is that the archive's integrity is independent of everything else. A release key is used by automation, on a schedule set by shipping, and is exposed to a build pipeline. Sharing one key would make the archive only as trustworthy as the release pipeline's worst day, and would mean a release-key rotation invalidated the chain of custody over evidence that has nothing to do with releases.

key_custody.rotation: A release key is rotated by publishing the new public key, signing the first release with both, and recording the changeover date. Nothing re-signs old artifacts: their signatures stay valid under the old key, which is why the timestamp matters more than the key's current status.
key_custody.where_it_lives:
A GitHub Actions *environment* secret, not a repository secret. ci.yml runs on push and pull_request, and a same-repository pull request receives repository secrets, so a repository-level signing key would be readable from any branch anyone pushes. The environment is what scopes it.

Scoping it to the environment is half the control; the other half is restricting which refs may deploy there. An environment with no deployment policy admits any branch, and a workflow file is something a branch can change -- so the key is as protected as the ability to push a branch. A tag policy of 'v*' closes that.

AMENDED 2026-09-11: this said 'an environment with required reviewers'. That was written assuming a team. Notrios is a solo project, and a required reviewer who is also the person triggering the run is a prompt rather than a second pair of eyes -- it would add a click per release and call it a control. The ref restriction is the instrument that actually works for one person, because it is preventive rather than a confirmation, and it does not depend on anybody being available.

CONFIGURED 2026-09-11: production admits exactly two refs -- branch 'main' and tag 'v*' -- where it previously admitted every ref. main is itself protected: required pull-request reviews, force pushes disabled. So the key is reachable only from a release tag, or from a branch that cannot be changed without a pull request and cannot be rewritten. The threat this control exists for -- a workflow file being something a branch can change -- is closed on both paths.

not_resolved_here: No key has been created. This item decides the policy; creating a production key before deciding what it is for, whose it is and how it rotates would invert that.
No release workflow exists yet. I6 builds the release evidence set and is where a signing step would first appear, under the constraints recorded here.
Whether the project publishes an apt repository. That would add a Release-file signature and a published key, and is a distribution decision rather than a signing one.
Windows and macOS remain deferred to post-v1.0 with the hardware they need, so their entries record a policy nobody can execute yet rather than a plan for this milestone.

platforms.mechanism: detached OpenPGP signature over each artifact and over SHA256SUMS, plus an RFC 3161 timestamp over the .deb's signature

not_chosen.apt repository InRelease signing: That is the right mechanism for an apt repository and this project does not publish one; v1.0 ships through a GitHub Release. If an apt repository is ever published, its Release file is signed and this entry gains a second mechanism rather than swapping.
not_chosen.dpkg-sig: apt does not verify a per-.deb signature on a file you downloaded, so it would look like protection while the command a user actually runs -- `apt install ./notrios.deb` -- checks nothing.

platforms.blocked_on: no arm64 machine. H6a left the arm64 package at level 2, structurally inspected, and v0.9 I3 installed only amd64. Signing an artifact nobody has run would attest its origin and say nothing about whether it works.
platforms.mechanism: identical to amd64; the policy does not differ by architecture

platforms.blocked_on: an OV or EV code-signing certificate from a CA, which requires an organisational identity check; EV additionally requires a hardware token or cloud HSM, which a hosted runner cannot hold without a signing service. And a native runner: H6a found a cross-built Windows artifact is level 1 evidence and nothing here can execute it.
platforms.mechanism: Authenticode over the installer and the executables, with an RFC 3161 timestamp so signatures outlive the certificate

platforms.blocked_on: Apple Developer Program membership, which is an owner account and cannot be delegated to this repository, and native hardware: H6a established nothing about macOS can be determined on this machine.
platforms.mechanism: Developer ID Application signature, then notarization with notarytool, then stapling the ticket so Gatekeeper accepts the artifact offline

prerequisite.detail: Met on 2026-09-11 by v1.0 J1: .github/workflows/release.yml builds the package with `make deb` and attests it with actions/attest-build-provenance. The validator derives this state from the workflows rather than reading it here, which is how the change was noticed -- writing the workflow made this record false and the gate said so.
prerequisite.permissions: id-token: write and attestations: write, declared on the job that needs them rather than inherited. performance/v0.9-i6/check_workflow_hardening.py refuses a workflow that declares no permissions at all, and least privilege means these two appear only where they are used.
prerequisite.proven: Statically. The workflow lints clean, passes the hardening and secret-exposure gates, and its two assertions were exercised locally against the real package. The attestation itself is unproven until a run produces one: it needs the runner's OIDC identity and cannot be exercised on a workstation.

verify: gh attestation trusted-root > trusted_root.jsonl   # for verifying offline later
provenance.what_it_attests: That a named workflow, running from a named commit, produced these exact bytes. Sigstore keyless signing binds a short-lived certificate to the workflow's OIDC identity and logs it, so the claim is verifiable by somebody who trusts GitHub and Sigstore rather than by somebody who has this project's public key.

why_it_does_not_replace_the_key.decision: ship both -- attestations for how it was built, a maintainer key for who stands behind it
why_it_does_not_replace_the_key.different_claims: An attestation says this artifact came out of that build. A detached OpenPGP signature says the holder of this key approved it. A reproducible build with impeccable provenance can still be a build of something nobody meant to ship.
why_it_does_not_replace_the_key.different_trust_roots: Attestation verification is rooted in GitHub and Sigstore and needs gh or cosign, plus a bundle and trusted root to work offline. `gpg --verify` needs a public key and nothing else -- which is the property this project's evidence reserve is built on, deliberately: exact OpenPGP and RFC 3161 identities rather than ambient trust.
why_it_does_not_replace_the_key.neither_is_checked_by_apt: `apt install ./notrios.deb` verifies neither. Verification stays a deliberate act the user takes before installing, which is why the installation page shows it as one.

timestamping.what_it_does_not_attest: When the software was built or the work was done. Only when the signature was stamped.
timestamping.why_it_matters: A signature proves who; a timestamp proves when, and keeps proving it after the key expires or is revoked. The same authority and the same pinned policy OID the evidence reserve already uses, verified by the same code path in evidence/verify_evidence.py, so there is one verification story rather than two.

what_this_is: What signing, notarization and timestamping mean for each platform this project ships or intends to ship, written so somebody who is not the author can carry it out or say why they cannot. Nothing signs a release today: scripts/build_deb.sh and scripts/package_release.sh produce unsigned artifacts, which is what v0.8 explicitly allowed for internal evidence.
